In field characteristic p, the binomial theorem gives (X−b)p=Xp−bp, since the intermediate binomial coefficients are divisible by the prime number p. If b∈F is a root of Xp−a, then bp=a, and hence
Xp−a=(X−b)pin F[X].​
(1)

b

Words: 93 Articles: 1
1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 93
b OurBigBook.com
Let α be a root in a splitting field. The preceding characteristic-p identity gives Xp−a=(X−α)p, so there is only one distinct root. If the polynomial were reducible over F, choose a monic proper factor g∈F[X] of degree d, with 1≤d<p. In the splitting field it must be g=(X−α)d. Its coefficient of Xd−1 is −dα, which belongs to F. Since d is nonzero and thus invertible in the field F, this forces α∈F, contradicting the absence of a root there. Therefore Xp−a is irreducible over F.

Suppose a rational function P(t)/Q(t)∈Fp​(t), with nonzero polynomials P,Q, had pth power t. Then P(t)p=tQ(t)p, so comparison of degrees would give pdegP=1+pdegQ, impossible modulo p. Thus Xp−t has no root in K, and part (b) proves it is irreducible.
In a splitting field containing α with αp=t,
Xp−t=(X−α)p.​
(2)
It has one distinct root with multiplicity p, so it is inseparable. This is the purely inseparable polynomial over a rational function field.

b

Words: 88 Articles: 1
1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 88
b OurBigBook.com
For a regular tetrahedron, rotations fixing a vertex rotate about the line from that vertex through the opposite face centre. Their angles are 0,2π/3,4π/3, so the stabilizer is a cyclic group of order three. Rotations act transitively on the four vertices, giving ∣G1​∣=4⋅3=12 by the orbit-stabilizer theorem.
For a cube, the corresponding axis is the body diagonal through the fixed vertex and its opposite. The three incident edges can be cyclically permuted by the same three angles, so again the stabilizer is cyclic of order three. The orbit has eight vertices. Hence
∣G1​∣=12,∣G2​∣=24.​
(5)

c

Words: 81 Articles: 1
1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 81
c OurBigBook.com
Realize the cube's vertices as (±1,±1,±1) and take the four with coordinate product +1. They form a regular tetrahedron, and their negatives form the other one. Every proper rotation of the first tetrahedron also permutes the negatives, hence is a cube rotation. This embeds G1​ as a subgroup of G2​.
The embedded group preserves each of these two four-vertex sets and acts transitively on each. Thus the resulting action on all eight cube vertices has two orbits, each of size four.

The fundamental theorem of arithmetic says that every integer n>1 is a product of prime numbers, uniquely up to reordering. Equivalently, n=∏p​pap​ for a unique family of nonnegative integer exponents, only finitely many of which are nonzero.

If the complete list of prime numbers were p1​,…,pk​, then N=p1​⋯pk​+1>1 would have a prime divisor by the fundamental theorem of arithmetic. No pi​ divides it, since N≡1(modpi​). This contradicts completeness of the list. Hence there are infinitely many prime numbers.

Every integer has one of the six residues 0,1,2,3,4,5 modulo 6. A prime number other than 2 or 3 is divisible by neither 2 nor 3, eliminating residues 0,2,3,4. Thus
p≡1 or −1(mod6).​
(6)
ii
Words: 97 Articles: 1
b OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 97
ii OurBigBook.com
Suppose there were only finitely many prime numbers congruent to 5 modulo 6, and list them as p1​,…,pk​. The list is nonempty since it contains 5. Let N=6p1​⋯pk​−1. It is greater than one and divisible by neither 2 nor 3. Every prime factor therefore has residue 1 or −1 modulo 6. Since N≡−1(mod6), at least one prime factor q must have residue −1. But N≡−1(modpi​) for every listed prime, so q is not on the list. This contradiction proves there are infinitely many primes congruent to 5 modulo 6.

The Lebesgue outer measure is
m∗(E)=inf{∑j​∣Ij​∣:E⊆⋃j​Ij​, Ij​ open intervals}.
(7)
The Lebesgue inner measure is m∗​(E)=sup{m(K):K⊆E, K compact}, with m∗​(∅)=0. For a bounded set inside a finite interval I, this is equivalently ∣I∣−m∗(I∖E).
A set is Lebesgue measurable if it satisfies Carathéodory's criterion:
m∗(A)=m∗(A∩E)+m∗(A∖E)for every A⊆R.​
(8)
For finite outer measure this is equivalent to equality of inner and outer measure. For a general unbounded set, an equivalent local criterion is m∗​(E∩[−n,n])=m∗(E∩[−n,n]) for every positive integer n. Merely writing m∗​(E)=m∗(E)=∞ would not establish measurability.

A null set has Lebesgue outer measure zero. Equivalently, for every ε>0 it can be covered by countably many open intervals whose total length is less than ε. Such a set is automatically Lebesgue measurable and has Lebesgue measure zero.

If A⊆E and E is a null set, every interval cover of E also covers A. Thus monotonicity of Lebesgue outer measure gives 0≤m∗(A)≤m∗(E)=0. Hence every subset of a null set is null, and in particular is Lebesgue measurable.

{x:f(x)>a} is Lebesgue measurable for every real a.​
(9)
These upper rays generate the Borel sigma-algebra, making this equivalent to requiring measurable inverse images of all Borel sets.

Solution
Words: 61
e OurBigBook.com
If a≥0, the set {f>a} is contained in E, since f=0 outside E. It is therefore a null set and is Lebesgue measurable. If a<0, its complement {f≤a} is contained in E and is measurable for the same reason. Complements of measurable sets are measurable. Thus every upper level set is measurable, proving f is a measurable function.

For sigma-finite measures, Tonelli's theorem states that the double integral of a nonnegative measurable function equals either iterated integral, allowing +∞. Fubini's theorem states that if a measurable function is absolutely integrable, its sections are integrable almost everywhere, both iterated integrals exist, and they equal the double integral.
Assign any value at (0,0), which does not affect Lebesgue integrability. Near that corner set s=x+y and t=(x−y)/(x+y). Then x=s(1+t)/2, y=s(1−t)/2, and the absolute Jacobian determinant is s/2. On 0<s<1, the full range is −1<t<1, so
∬x+y<1​∣F(x,y)∣dxdy=21​∫01​s2−αds∫−11​∣t∣dt=21​∫01​s2−αds.
(10)
The remaining part of the unit square has x+y≥1 and is harmless. The improper power integral is finite precisely when α<3. Under the given restriction,
F is Lebesgue integrable exactly for 2<α<3.​
(11)
For those values, the change (x,y)↦(y,x) preserves the square and changes the sign of F. Absolute integrability justifies this change of variables, giving
∬R2​F(x,y)dxdy=0.​
(12)
For α≥3 the positive and negative parts each diverge, so symmetry does not define a Lebesgue integral.

Solution

Words: 152
1 OurBigBook.com
An open cover of a topological space is a collection of open subsets whose union is the whole space. A compact space is one for which every open cover admits a finite subcover. The subspace topology on A⊆Y consists of sets A∩O with O open in Y.
Let {Uj​} cover f(X) by relatively open sets, and write Uj​=f(X)∩Oj​ with Oj​ open in Y. By continuity, {f−1(Oj​)} is an open cover of X. A finite subcollection covers X by compactness, and its corresponding Uj​ cover f(X). Thus a continuous image of a compact space is compact.
For an image that is not closed, take X to be a singleton and Y={0,1} with the indiscrete topology. Send the sole point to 0. This map is continuous and X is compact, while f(X)={0} is not closed in Y, whose only closed sets are ∅ and Y. A Hausdorff hypothesis on the target would exclude this example.

a OurBigBook.com
A sequence xn​ converges to x if every open neighbourhood of x contains all sufficiently late terms. A Hausdorff space separates any two distinct points by disjoint open neighbourhoods.
If a sequence had distinct limits x,y in a Hausdorff space, choose disjoint open neighbourhoods U of x and V of y. Convergence to each limit implies that all sufficiently late terms lie in both U and V, contradicting U∩V=∅. Hence a convergent sequence in a Hausdorff space has a unique limit.

Words: 84 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 84
b OurBigBook.com
The product topology on X×Y has as a basis of a topology the rectangles U×V with U open in X and V open in Y; arbitrary unions of such rectangles are its open sets.
For distinct points (x1​,y1​),(x2​,y2​), at least one coordinate differs. If x1​=x2​, disjoint open neighbourhoods U1​,U2​ in the Hausdorff space X give disjoint open neighbourhoods U1​×Y,U2​×Y of the two points. If the second coordinates differ instead, use X×V1​,X×V2​. Thus a product of two Hausdorff spaces is Hausdorff.

For the quotient map q:X→X/∼, the quotient topology is defined by
U⊆X/∼ open⟺q−1(U) open in X.
(13)
Take the Hausdorff space X=R and identify two numbers precisely when they are both rational or both irrational. The quotient has two points. The inverse images of its singleton subsets are Q and R∖Q, neither of which is open in R, since each is dense and has dense complement. Hence the quotient has the indiscrete topology and is not Hausdorff.

A k-dimensional embedded submanifold of Rn is a subset M such that near each p∈M there is a smooth diffeomorphism of ambient open neighbourhoods that sends M to the coordinate plane Rk×{0}n−k. More precisely, for some open U∋p and diffeomorphism Φ:U→V⊆Rn,
Φ(M∩U)=V∩(Rk×{0}n−k).
(14)
Thus locally the subset has k freely varying smooth coordinates.

A tangent vector to M at p is a velocity γ′(0) of a smooth curve γ:(−ε,ε)→M with γ(0)=p. The tangent space is the set of all such velocities:
Tp​M={γ′(0):γ(0)=p, γ a smooth curve in M}.​
(15)
It is a k-dimensional linear subspace of Rn; for a local parametrization ϕ, it is the image of the injective derivative Dϕ at the corresponding parameter point.

Let P=Fy′​ and Q=Fy′′​. For a smooth variation y+εη, the first variation is
δJ=∫ab​(Fy​η+Pη′+Qη′′)dx=∫ab​(Fy​−P′+Q′′)ηdx+[(P−Q′)η+Qη′]ab​.
(19)
Here the last expression follows by two integrations by parts. Taking variations supported in the interior and applying the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations gives the Euler-Lagrange equation for a second-derivative functional:
Fy​−dxd​Fy′​+dx2d2​Fy′′​=0.​
(20)
If both endpoint values and slopes are free, their independent variations force the natural boundary conditions for second-derivative functionals
Q=0,P−Q′=0at a,b.​
(21)
If an endpoint value or slope is fixed instead, its corresponding variation vanishes and the associated natural condition is not required.
For H=y′′Q−y′(Q′−P)−F, differentiate using the chain rule:
H′=y′(P′−Q′′−Fy​)−Fx​.
(22)
The Euler-Lagrange equation cancels the first term. Consequently H′=−Fx​, and if there is no explicit x dependence,
H=y′′Fy′′​+y′(Fy′​−(Fy′′​)′)−F is constant.​
(23)
This is a Beltrami identity for a second-derivative functional.

Solution

Words: 168
1 OurBigBook.com
A streamline is a curve whose tangent is parallel to the instantaneous fluid velocity field. In steady flow one may parametrize it by dr/ds=u(r). Dotting the steady Euler equations with u eliminates the cross-product term, since u⋅((∇×u)×u)=0. Hence
u⋅∇(p+21​ρ∣u∣2)=0,​
(30)
which is Bernoulli's principle along each streamline.
For the supplied field, xu+yv=0, so along a streamline
dsd​(x2+y2)=2xu+2yv=0.
(31)
Writing r2=x2+y2, the tangential speed is vθ​=−br+c/r and the radial speed is zero. Both r and ∣u∣2=(−br+c/r)2 are constant around each nonstagnant circular streamline. The Bernoulli quantity is constant there, so the pressure is constant on every such circle.
If a circle is wholly stagnant, the same conclusion follows directly from the steady Euler equations: on it u=0 and ∇∣u∣2=0, hence ∇p=0. Equivalently the radial momentum equation gives ∇p=ρ(−br+c/r)2er​/r and no angular pressure variation, including at zero tangential speed. Thus p is constant on x2+y2=a2 for every nonzero a, with no exception for a stagnation circle.

Solution

Words: 134
2 OurBigBook.com
Use the convention that positive vortex strength is counterclockwise and complex velocity is u−iv. A complex potential of a two-dimensional potential flow for the superposed uniform flow and two point vortices is
W(z)=Uz+2πiΓ​log(z−a)−2πiΓ​log(z+a).​
(32)
Local choices of logarithm branch change no velocity. Differentiation gives
W′(z)=U−π(z2−a2)iΓa​.
(33)
For nonzero vortex strength and U>0, its two zeros are
z±​=±a2+πUiΓa​​.​
(34)
The number under the square root is nonzero, so these are distinct stagnation points, neither at a vortex.
A free point vortex moves with the velocity induced by the other vortex and the background, omitting its own singular field. At either vortex, the other induces vertical velocity −Γ/(4πa), while the background contributes (U,0). Their velocities are therefore equal. The Neyman-Pearson lemma concerns testing a simple null density f0​ against a simple alternative f1​. A test that rejects where f1​/f0​>c, accepts where the ratio is below c, and if necessary randomizes on the boundary to have null rejection probability α, is a most powerful test among tests of size at most α. Thus a likelihood-ratio threshold maximizes power at the specified simple alternative. The boundary randomization is relevant for discrete distributions.

gR​(v)=rq(v)(1−1−v2​)​=2r1−1−v2​​,−1<v<1.
(83)
If any of the first n trials accepts, the returned value has target density f. If all n reject, which has probability rn, the forced return is the final rejected proposal and has density gR​. Thus the capped algorithm has density
fn​=(1−rn)f+rngR​.​
(84)
It is biased toward the ends of the interval, where rejection is most likely, and has too little mass near the centre. The bias disappears geometrically as the trial cap increases. This is bias from returning a rejected proposal after a rejection-sampling cap.
Conditional on acceptance before the nth trial, however, the returned value has exactly the semicircle law. For each possible first successful trial its value has density f, independently of the number of previous failures; a mixture of these identical conditional laws remains f.

The bisection method begins with a finite interval [a,b] on which the continuous function has opposite signs at its endpoints. The intermediate value theorem guarantees a root inside. Evaluate at the midpoint m=(a+b)/2. If f(m)=0, stop. Otherwise retain the half whose endpoints have opposite signs and repeat. An endpoint that is already a root is returned immediately. The nested intervals retain a root and their lengths halve, so their midpoints converge to a root.
ii
Words: 81 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 81
ii OurBigBook.com
If the starting length is L=b−a, then after k interval halvings the current midpoint is at most L/2k+1 from some root remaining in the bracket. Thus, with the midpoint returned after those halvings, it suffices to take
k≥max(0,⌈log2​2ϵL​⌉).​
(89)
If iterations instead count midpoint evaluations starting with the initial midpoint as evaluation one, the usual bound is n≥⌈log2​(L/ϵ)⌉, with at least one evaluation unless an endpoint root has already been found. Stating the counting convention avoids an apparent one-step discrepancy.

b

Words: 176 Articles: 1
1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 176
b OurBigBook.com
The following R function uses the factored polynomial for evaluation, handles endpoint and midpoint roots, and returns a midpoint only once its error bound is at most eps:
bisect <- function(a, b, eps = 1e-8, maxiter = 1000L) {
  f <- function(x) x * (x - 1) * (x - 2) * (x - 5)
  stopifnot(length(a) == 1L, length(b) == 1L,
            is.finite(a), is.finite(b), a < b,
            length(eps) == 1L, is.finite(eps), eps > 0)
  fa <- f(a)
  fb <- f(b)
  if (fa == 0) return(a)
  if (fb == 0) return(b)
  if (sign(fa) == sign(fb)) stop("Endpoints must bracket a sign change")
  for (i in seq_len(maxiter)) {
    m <- a + (b - a) / 2
    fm <- f(m)
    if (fm == 0 || (b - a) / 2 <= eps) return(m)
    if (sign(fm) == sign(fa)) {
      a <- m
      fa <- fm
    } else {
      b <- m
    }
  }
  stop("Iteration limit reached")
}
Each update preserves the sign-changing bracket, and the stopping bound is the half-width of that bracket. Thus continuity and the intermediate value theorem justify the returned root approximation.

At the left endpoint f(−1)=36>0. If b=2, the endpoint is exactly a root and the function above immediately returns 2. For 2<b≤4, f(b)<0, so the first midpoint is m=(b−1)/2.
If 2<b<3, then 1/2<m<1 and f(m)<0. The first retained bracket is [−1,m], containing only the root zero, so the iterates converge to zero. If b=3, the first midpoint is exactly the root one and is returned. If 3<b≤4, then 1<m≤3/2 and f(m)>0. The retained bracket is [m,b], containing only the root two, so the iterates converge to two. Hence
returned root=⎩⎨⎧​2,0,1,2,​b=2,2<b<3,b=3,3<b≤4.​​
(90)
This illustrates root selection by bisection with multiple roots in the initial bracket: bisection guarantees a root, but which root it chooses depends discontinuously on the starting endpoint.
